table.title: [Estimated Population of China at Various Dates]
table.caption_extra: The subjoined tables show the estimated population at various dates (obtained from various sources and abstracted chiefly from "The Middle Kingdom") and the latest official estimates of the population:—
transcriber_notes: Reading order: the table reads across each printed line, left pair then right pair, and then down to the next line; read that way the 26 dates form one chronological series (1381, 1412, 1580, 1662, 1668, 1710, 1711, 1736, 1743, 1753, ,, , 1760, ,, , ,, , 1761, 1762, 1790, 1792, 1812, ,, , ,, , 1842, 1868, 1881, 1882, 1885). A ditto mark ',,' therefore repeats the year of the entry just before it in that order: the left-hand ',,' on line 6 is 1753, the ',,' marks on line 7 are both 1760, and the ',,' marks on lines 10 (right) and 11 (left) are 1812. So 1753 has two figures, 1760 three and 1812 three; 1710 has two figures on one line.

Printed as two side-by-side blocks of 13 lines each, each block a year followed by leaders (dots) and a population figure; reproduced as four columns, left block in columns 1-2, right block in columns 3-4, row i of each block on the same line as printed. No blank cells: both blocks have 13 lines.
No column headings are printed; 'Year' / 'Population' are supplied. 'A.D.' (small caps) is printed only before the first year of each block.
1710 is printed with two figures on one line, '23,312,200 & 27,241,129'; kept in one cell as printed.
No totals, braces, footnote marks or source notes in the table itself; the source is given in the preceding sentence (caption_extra).
All 26 figures re-read from tight crops of leaf n21 (printed p. 2); none unreadable.
table.context: The section opens (p. 1) by saying that a census by Western methods "has never yet been attempted in China, and consequently estimates of the total population have varied to an extraordinary degree", and names the Minchengpu (Ministry of Interior) census of 1910 as, until the previous year, the nearest approach to a reliable estimate. On p. 2 the book gives these figures as the estimated population at various dates "obtained from various sources and abstracted chiefly from 'The Middle Kingdom'", naming no source for any single figure. The table is read across each line and then down, which puts the dates in order; the ditto marks (,,) repeat the year before them, so the book gives two estimates for 1710 and 1753 and three each for 1760 and 1812. After the table the book turns to the 1919-20 Post Office estimate, printed on p. 3 with the 1885 Census and the Minchengpu census for comparison.
